title: Maximum Candies Allocated to K Children
statement:
Each value `candies[i]` is the size of a pile of candies. A pile may be cut into any number of smaller piles of any sizes, but two piles can never be combined. There are `k` children, and every child must receive the same amount, all of it taken from a single pile; candies left over are simply not handed out.

Return the largest amount every child can receive. If there is no way to give each child at least one candy, return `0`.
notes:
## Intuition

Ask the question the other way round: if every child gets exactly `share` candies, how many children can be served? A pile of size `p` yields `floor(p / share)` portions, so the count is easy to compute. The count only shrinks as `share` grows, so the feasible shares form a prefix `1..answer`, and binary search can find its end. Trying every share one by one would also work, but the largest pile can be 10^7.

## Approach

1. Search shares between `low = 1` and `high` = the largest pile; `best = 0` covers the case where nothing works.
2. Take the middle `share` and add up `floor(pile / share)` over all piles into `children`.
3. If `children >= k`, the share is achievable: record it in `best` and look higher.
4. Otherwise the share is too big: look lower.
5. When the range is empty, `best` is the largest achievable share.

## Example 1, step by step

`candies = [5, 8, 6]`, `k = 3`, so the range is 1..8.

- `share = 4`: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 children, enough; `best = 4`, range 5..8.
- `share = 6`: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 children, too few; range 5..5.
- `share = 5`: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 children, enough; `best = 5`, range 6..5 is empty.

The answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log M), where M is the largest pile: each of the log M rounds scans every pile once.
- Space: O(1) beyond the input.

## Pitfalls

- Start `low` at 1, not 0, or `floor(pile / 0)` divides by zero.
- `k` can be 10^12, larger than the total number of candies; then the answer is `0`, which `best`'s starting value already returns.
- In Java or C, keep `children` in a 64-bit integer: the sum of portions can reach 10^12.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `low`, `high` | the range of shares still undecided |
| `best` | largest share proven achievable so far |
| `share` | the candidate number of candies per child |
| `children` | how many children can get `share` candies |
| `pile` | the size of the current pile |

narration.2: The smallest share worth testing is one candy per child.
narration.3: No child can get more than the biggest pile, so that bounds the search.
narration.4: If no share works, every child gets zero candies.
narration.6: Keep halving the range of candidate shares until it is empty.
narration.7: Test the share in the middle of the range.
narration.9: Walk through every pile to count the portions it can provide.
narration.10: A pile of this size can be cut into floor(pile / share) full portions.
narration.12: Are there enough portions for all k children?
narration.13: Yes: this share is achievable, so remember it.
narration.14: Try to give each child even more.
narration.16: No: the share is too large, so search the smaller half.
narration.19: The last achievable share found is the maximum.
